title: A failing readiness probe takes a Pod out of rotation without restarting it
dek: A short Japanese talk, translated here, separates two Kubernetes probes by what happens when they fail. Its terminal shows the readiness half.

sections.heading: Two probes, two different responses to failure

blocks.text: The speaker sets out to explain how readiness and liveness probes differ [@j-intro]. The answer, in translation, is about consequences. A failing readiness probe removes the Pod from the Service's endpoints but does not restart it [@j-ready]:
readinessプローブが失敗すると、Podはサービスのエンドポイントから外されますが、再起動はされません。

A failing liveness probe is different: the kubelet restarts the container [@j-live]. The Kubernetes documentation says the same. A failed readiness probe removes the Pod's IP address from the EndpointSlices of matching Services, while repeated liveness failures make the kubelet restart the container [@k8s].

sections.heading: Each probe asks a different question, so each failure has a different remedy

blocks.text: The speaker's distinction is easiest to hold if each probe is read as a question the kubelet keeps asking. A readiness probe asks whether this Pod should receive traffic right now. A liveness probe asks whether the container is stuck in a way that only a restart will fix. A startup probe asks whether the application has finished starting. The consequences the talk describes follow directly from those questions [@j-ready; @j-live; @j-startup].

A failed readiness check has a gentle remedy: stop sending this Pod new requests. Nothing is killed, and the Pod keeps running so that it can recover by itself. The Kubernetes documentation describes readiness checks as running for the whole life of the container, not only at start [@k8s]. A Pod can therefore leave rotation and rejoin it later, for example while it waits for a dependency or works through a backlog. The talk does not show that recovery; this is what the documented behavior implies.

A failed liveness check has a harsh remedy: the kubelet restarts the container [@j-live]. That is the right response to a deadlock or a corrupted in-memory state, where waiting will never help. It is the wrong response to a slow database, because a restart throws away a working process and adds start-up load at the moment the system is already struggling. This is our reading of the tradeoff, not a claim the speaker makes.

sections.heading: The terminal shows a Pod that is running, not ready, and never restarted

blocks.text: On screen, the configuration sets a readiness probe on `/ready` every five seconds and a liveness probe on `/healthz` with a failure threshold of three [@j-config]. The Pod listing then shows `READY 0/1`, `STATUS Running`, and `RESTARTS 0` [@j-pods].
That is what a failing readiness probe looks like: out of rotation, still running, not restarted. The video does not say which probe failed, so this reading is ours.

sections.heading: Reading the Pod listing column by column

blocks.text: The terminal frame carries more information than its single line suggests [@j-pods]. `READY 0/1` counts containers: zero of the Pod's one container currently passes its readiness check. `STATUS Running` says the container process is up; it is not a health verdict. `RESTARTS 0` says the kubelet has not restarted the container since the Pod started.

Put together, the three columns rule things out. A liveness failure would push the restart count up, and it is zero. A crashed process would usually show a status other than Running. What remains is a process that runs but is not ready, which is the readiness case the speaker describes. That chain of reasoning is ours; the video shows the listing but does not narrate it.

sections.heading: Slow starters get a third probe

blocks.text: For slow-starting apps, the speaker calls a startup probe 定石 (*joseki*), translated here as the standard move [@j-startup]. The word comes from the game of Go, where it names an established sequence of play. It is stronger than a habit and weaker than a rule, so we keep the original term.
The documentation agrees that startup probes suit containers that take a long time to come into service, and that liveness and readiness checks wait until the startup probe succeeds [@k8s].

The reason a third probe helps is a timing conflict. Without it, a slow starter forces a choice: give the liveness probe a long initial delay or a lenient threshold, which also slows the detection of a real deadlock later, or keep liveness strict and watch the kubelet restart the container before it ever finishes starting. A startup probe separates the two phases, so start-up can be slow and liveness can still be strict once the application is up. This is our explanation of the design, consistent with the documented ordering.

The Go meaning of joseki carries a useful warning too. Go players have a proverb that learning joseki costs you two stones, because a standard sequence played without understanding why it works goes wrong when the position differs. A startup probe copied with someone else's thresholds has the same weakness: the shape is standard, but the numbers must fit your own start-up time.

sections.heading: How to find out which probe is failing in your own cluster

blocks.text: The video stops at one listing. In practice you would confirm the diagnosis before changing configuration. These steps are standard Kubernetes practice, not something the talk shows:

items: Run `kubectl describe pod` and read the Events at the bottom. Failed probes are reported there, and the message names which probe failed.
Watch the RESTARTS column over a few minutes. A count that keeps climbing points to liveness; a count that stays at zero while READY stays at 0/1 points to readiness.
Check the Service's EndpointSlices to see whether the Pod's address is listed. A Pod that fails readiness should be missing from them.
Call the probe endpoints yourself, for example through `kubectl port-forward`, and compare the response with what the probe expects.

sections.heading: A rule that transfers: match the probe to the remedy you want

blocks.text: The transferable rule is to choose a probe by the remedy, not by the symptom. If the right response to a problem is to stop sending traffic until it clears, it belongs in readiness. If the right response is to restart the process, it belongs in liveness, and the check should test only the process itself, never a shared dependency. If the problem is simply that the application takes a long time to start, that is what a startup probe is for, which is the speaker's joseki.

Two cautions apply before reusing the speaker's configuration. The timeout they chose is unknown, so copying the rest of the file without it leaves the most sensitive setting undecided. And the English here is a translation of Japanese speech: where the wording matters, read the original segments on the transcript page rather than our rendering.

brief.question: What happens to a Pod when each probe fails?

evidence.text: The speaker says a failing readiness probe removes the Pod from Service endpoints without a restart, and a failing liveness probe restarts the container.
The Pod listing shows READY 0/1, STATUS Running, RESTARTS 0.
Kubernetes documents the same failure responses and recommends startup probes for slow starters.
Slow-starting apps should use a startup probe (the speaker's 定石).
The timeout value the speaker set is inaudible and not shown.

proposals.text: Use readiness for warm-up and dependency checks, and keep liveness for states a restart actually fixes, such as deadlock.
proposals.risks: A liveness probe that checks dependencies can restart healthy containers under load.

proposals.text: Recover the timeout from the speaker's slides or repository before reusing the configuration.

limitations: The English is a translation of Japanese speech, not the speaker's words; 定石 is kept in the original because its translation is lossy.
Evaluation fixture: generated slides and a tone for audio, so this article does not test transcription or translation accuracy.
The timeout value is unknown, and the video does not show which probe failed.
